title: Mass Defect and Binding Energy
short: A nucleus weighs less than its separate parts, and the missing mass times c² is its binding energy.
trouble: Students think a nucleus weighs more than its separate protons and neutrons, or forget to change atomic mass units to kilograms before using E = mc².

blocks.html: Weigh a helium-4 atom and compare it with two hydrogen atoms plus two neutrons: the atom is lighter. The missing mass became the energy that holds the nucleus together, by $E = mc^2$. This connects stability with the energy of fission and fusion, and uses scientific notation throughout.

Mass defect: $\Delta m = Z\,m(^1\mathrm{H}) + N\,m_n - m(\text{atom})$. Binding energy: $E_b = \Delta mc^2$, which is $931.5\ \text{MeV}$ for every $1\ \text{u}$ of mass defect. Binding energy per nucleon, $E_b/A$, measures how tightly a nucleus is held; it peaks near iron and nickel at about $8.8\ \text{MeV}$.

Bound systems have less energy than their separate parts: energy is released when they form, and must be supplied to pull them apart. Relativity says energy has mass, so the bound nucleus weighs less. Using hydrogen-1 atoms (a proton plus an electron) instead of bare protons means the electrons are counted on both sides, so atomic masses from tables can be used directly. Because $E_b/A$ peaks near $A = 56$–62, fusing light nuclei moves up the curve and releases energy, and so does splitting heavy ones.

blocks.name: ch-nuclide
blocks.cap: Binding energy per nucleon across the nuclides. It climbs steeply for light nuclei, peaks near iron and nickel, and falls slowly for the heaviest.

blocks.title: Helium-4
blocks.q: Find the mass defect, binding energy and binding energy per nucleon of helium-4 (atomic mass $4.002603\ \text{u}$). Use $m(^1\mathrm{H}) = 1.007825\ \text{u}$ and $m_n = 1.008665\ \text{u}$.

blocks.title: In joules and per mole
blocks.q: Express helium-4's binding energy in joules per nucleus and in kJ/mol ($1\ \text{u} = 1.6605 \times 10^{-27}\ \text{kg}$, $c = 3.00 \times 10^8\ \text{m/s}$).
steps: Per mole: $$(4.54 \times 10^{-12})(6.022 \times 10^{23}) = 2.73 \times 10^{12}\ \text{J/mol} = 2.73 \times 10^{9}\ \text{kJ/mol}$$ millions of times a chemical bond energy.

blocks.title: Iron-56
blocks.q: Iron-56 has atomic mass $55.934936\ \text{u}$. Find its binding energy per nucleon.
steps: $E_b = (0.528464)(931.5) = 492.3\ \text{MeV}$; per nucleon $492.3/56 = 8.79\ \text{MeV}$, near the top of the curve.

blocks.html: Thinking a nucleus weighs more than its separate protons and neutrons, or using $E = mc^2$ with the mass still in atomic mass units. The nucleus is always lighter, and $c^2$ in $\text{m}^2/\text{s}^2$ needs mass in kilograms to give joules. Check: a binding energy in joules per nucleus should be around $10^{-12}$ to $10^{-10}\ \text{J}$.
